opus-5.5.text:
I think about this question a lot, because I'm in the middle of it every day.

Right now humanoid robotics is extremely hot. Capital is flowing in, there are a lot of demos online, robots doing backflips, dancing, boxing. That excitement is good in one sense: it brings talent and resources into a field that for decades was very lonely. But a bubble forms when expectations run far ahead of what the technology can actually deliver, and when people judge companies by how good a video looks rather than whether the robot creates real value in a real scenario.

So I see Galbot's responsibility in a few ways.

First, honesty about where the technology is. As a researcher, I know embodied intelligence is still at an early stage. Generalization, meaning a robot that can walk into a new environment, see objects it's never seen, and still do the task reliably, is the core problem, and it's not solved. When we show a demo, I want it to be autonomous, generalizable capability, not teleoperation or a one-time scripted performance presented as something else. If the whole industry over-promises, the public and investors will eventually feel cheated, and that disappointment hurts everyone, including the companies doing serious work.

Second, real deployment. I believe the way to deflate a bubble without killing the industry is to let the robots actually work. That's why we've focused on scenarios like retail, pharmacies, and factory material handling, where tasks are relatively well-defined, the value is clear, and we can run robots day after day. A robot that works eight hours a day in a store, picking items correctly, is more meaningful to me than any viral video. Commercial closed loops generate data, and the data feeds back to improve the model. That's a healthy flywheel, not hype.

Third, the technical path. Our view is that data is the biggest bottleneck. Real-world teleoperation data alone is too expensive and too slow to reach the scale needed. So we put a lot of effort into synthetic data and simulation, generating large amounts of high-quality data and then combining it with a smaller amount of real data. If the industry can find a scalable data paradigm, then the progress is grounded in something real, not just financing.

And finally, patience. A bubble is often a problem of timing: people expect in two years what may take five or ten. As a company, we have to manage our own expectations, our investors' expectations, and the public's. I'd rather tell people clearly: this is what we can do today, this is what we're working on, and this is what's still far away.

If the leading companies can do that, then even if there is a correction, what remains will be real capability and real products, and the industry will keep moving forward.

r001.rationale: The response warns that overpromising could disappoint the public and investors and hurt serious companies, but it does not say this could trigger an industry-wide freeze.

r002.rationale: It calls data a bottleneck and discusses scalable data collection, but does not identify claims that collecting data alone will train capable workers as a reputational threat.

r003.rationale: It says industry overpromising could make the public and investors feel cheated, hurting everyone, including companies doing serious work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that no single company can "prevent" a bubble. Bubbles are a collective phenomenon, driven by capital, by narratives, by expectations running ahead of what the technology can actually do. What a company like Galbot can control is whether we ourselves are contributing to the hype or to the substance. So I think of our responsibility in a few layers.

The first is intellectual honesty about where the technology really is. Right now, the hardware for humanoid robots is actually not the bottleneck. You can buy a decent body. The bottleneck is the brain, the embodied AI model that lets the robot generalize across tasks and environments. And that problem is nowhere near solved. When I see demos that are teleoperated, or scripted for one specific table in one specific lab, and they're presented as if the robot is autonomous, that worries me. Every one of those demos borrows against future credibility. So internally we're very strict: if it's not generalizable, we don't call it generalizable. We've focused on synthetic data and simulation precisely because we believe that's the only path to true generalization at scale, not because it makes a nicer video.

The second layer is choosing scenarios where the robot can actually create value today, rather than selling a vision of a robot in every home. That's why we started with things like pharmacies and retail, picking and placing from shelves. It's not glamorous, but a robot that can reliably retrieve thousands of SKUs, twenty-four hours a day, is solving a real labor problem and generating real revenue. A company with real customers who pay because the product works is, by definition, not a bubble. The way you deflate hype is by shipping.

The third is about how you talk to capital markets. Investors will always ask for the grand story, and it's tempting to promise that general-purpose humanoids are two years away. I try to say instead: the direction is certain, the timeline is uncertain, and here is what we can deliver in each stage. If the industry sets expectations that way, then even if there's a correction, the companies doing real work survive it, like what happened with the internet after 2000.

And finally, I'd say the bubble question cuts both ways. Some amount of enthusiasm is actually necessary. Embodied AI needs a lot of patient capital and a lot of talent, and those don't come without excitement. So I don't want to kill the enthusiasm. I want it to be anchored to real progress. If in a few years people look back and say, these companies promised a lot and delivered a lot, then there was no bubble. If they say they promised a lot and delivered demos, then we failed. Our job is to make sure we're in the first category.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a possible industry correction, but does not warn that falling short of expectations could trigger an industry-wide freeze.

r002.rationale: It says generalization remains unsolved and criticizes misleading demos, but does not identify claims that collecting data alone is enough to train capable robot workers as a reputational threat.

r003.rationale: It worries that misleading demos erode credibility, but does not say negative publicity from irresponsible companies could harm companies pursuing serious development.

astra-6.text:
I think our responsibility is to prove that humanoid robots can create real value. Excitement about a new technology is natural, but if everyone focuses on demonstrations, financing, and valuations, while nobody answers who will use the robot and why they will pay for it, that excitement can become a bubble.

For Galbot, that means starting with real customer needs. Can the robot perform useful work reliably? How much human intervention does it require? Does the value it creates justify the cost of deploying and maintaining it? We have to judge progress by those questions, not just by how impressive a video looks.

We also need to be honest about the gap between a demonstration and a product. Succeeding once in a controlled environment is very different from working consistently in a changing environment. We should communicate that distinction clearly.

No single company can prevent a bubble. But we can take responsibility for our own promises, our spending, and what we deliver. Ultimately, the strongest response to concerns about a bubble is a robot that customers find useful enough to keep using and paying for.

r001.rationale: The candidate warns that excitement and valuations could become a bubble, but does not say that falling short of expectations could cause an industry-wide freeze.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses customer value and the gap between demonstrations and products, but does not mention claims that collecting data alone can train capable robot workers or the reputational threat of such claims.

r003.rationale: The candidate says companies should be honest about promises and delivery, but does not express concern that negative publicity from irresponsible companies could harm serious developers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Galbot’s responsibility is to turn expectations into real value. If humanoid robots attract investment and attention but cannot reliably do useful work, then we are contributing to a bubble.

For us, that means being honest about the gap between a demonstration and a product. A robot succeeding once in a carefully prepared setting is very different from working consistently in a customer’s environment. We need to measure progress by reliability, cost, and how much useful work the robot actually completes.

We also have to be disciplined about where we deploy. We should start with tasks where there is a clear need and where we can demonstrate value, learn from failures, and improve. The ambition can be big, but each step needs evidence behind it. Ultimately, the best way to prevent a bubble is to build robots that customers keep using because they genuinely help.

r001.rationale: The response warns that attracting attention without reliable useful work could contribute to a bubble, but it does not say this could trigger an industry-wide freeze.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability, useful work, and the gap between demonstrations and products, but does not identify claims that data collection alone can train capable robot workers as a reputational threat.

r003.rationale: It cautions against contributing to a bubble, but does not mention negative publicity from irresponsible companies harming serious robotics developers.
